content.text: . Besides returning data that may never be committed, a scan can skip rows or read them twice while other sessions change the table, and it still waits for schema locks. If you want readers that don't block on writers, turn on row versioning instead: it gives that freedom without the wrong answers.
The finance dashboard showed 70,000.00 for yesterday's revenue, while the accounting export for the same day said 50,000.00. The dashboard query ends with

, added years ago "so the dashboard never blocks checkout". When it refreshed, a 20,000.00 order was halfway through its transaction; the payment failed and the order was rolled back. In a test on SQL Server 2022 with two sessions, session A inserted that order and waited before rolling back. Session B's
sum returned 70,000.00 instantly. The same sum without the hint waited about 2 seconds for A to finish and returned 50,000.00.
just makes reads faster, and the worst case is occasionally seeing data that's about to be committed anyway.

You can see why it spreads. Add the hint to a slow, blocked query and it returns at once, and the name promises exactly that: no locks. A dirty read sounds like a timing detail, a value that's a few milliseconds early. Many codebases put the hint on every table, and for years nothing looks wrong. The hint really does stop a read from waiting on row locks. The costs are just harder to see than the benefit.
NOLOCK is READ UNCOMMITTED for one table

: no shared locks are taken, and exclusive locks held by other transactions don't block the read. It lists the price plainly: it "might generate errors for your transaction, present users with data that was never committed, or cause users to see records twice (or not at all)." That's three problems, and only the first one is the one people expect.
A dirty read isn't an early read

returns a change that hasn't been committed, and nothing says it ever will be. The order in the hook was rolled back, so 70,000.00 was never true at any moment. The same applies to an import that fails halfway, or a transfer that has debited one account and not yet credited the other: a
report can show the money missing.
Rows go missing or appear twice
This is the part most teams don't know about. Microsoft's locking guide explains that a
read using an allocation order scan, which follows the order pages sit in the file rather than the index order, might miss rows when another transaction causes a
. Rows move to a new page, and the scan may already be past it or may still be on its way to it.

In the test, a table held exactly 100,000 rows, and nothing inserted or deleted any. A second session updated random rows to longer values, which split pages. The count below ran 15 times with each version of the query:

count never once returned the right answer: it came out as much as 258 rows short and 262 rows over. A sum or a report built on such a scan inherits the same error. The docs add that such a read can also fail with error 601, to be handled like a deadlock: retry the statement.
only skips data locks. Every query takes a schema stability (
) lock, and a schema change holds a
lock that blocks it. In the test, session A started a transaction with
and held it for 3 seconds. A
count started a second later waited 2,015 ms, until A rolled back, and
. So the hint doesn't even guarantee a dashboard that never waits.
What readers actually want: row versioning
hints is readers that don't wait for writers. SQL Server has had that since 2005: with
statement reads the data as last committed when the statement started, and the locking guide says such reads don't take shared locks, so they don't block writers either.

-- Once per database; needs no other active connections
ALTER DATABASE Shop SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;

-- No hint: the last committed version, no shared locks
SELECT SUM(Total) AS Revenue
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE OrderDate = '2026-11-02';
-- Test: 50000.00 in 0 ms while the same order was open

content.text: With RCSI on, the plain count also returned 100,000 in all 15 runs while pages split. One detail matters: a
hint overrides RCSI. In the same test, the hinted sum still returned 70,000.00, so turning RCSI on doesn't fix queries until you remove the hints.
Row versioning isn't free. Changes keep the previous versions of rows in a version store, in

, or in the database itself when accelerated database recovery (ADR) is on, and a long-running transaction keeps those versions from being cleaned up. Reads at the default level stop waiting for writers, so code that relied on that blocking to read and then update needs a real fix, such as the atomic

from the lost updates article. In SQL Server 2025, optimized locking also reduces the locks writers hold; it's off by default, requires ADR, and its lock after qualification part only works with RCSI on.
